Maya carried the box up the stairs two at a time. Inside, wrapped in yesterday's newspaper, was the gold statue with "MVP" stamped on its base.

"Aren't you putting it on the shelf?" her mother asked from the doorway.

Maya glanced at the empty spot next to her brother's old trophies. Then she thought of Priya, who had played the whole season with a sprained wrist and never once complained. When the coach read Maya's name at the banquet, Priya had clapped louder than anyone. Her eyes had been red the entire time.

"Maybe later," Maya said. She slid the box under her bed, next to the cleats she had outgrown, and pulled the blanket down so it hung all the way to the floor.

That night, she texted Priya: "You were the real MVP. Seriously." She stared at the screen until three dots appeared, then disappeared, then appeared again.
prompt: Why does Maya put the trophy under her bed?
choices: She thinks her friend deserved the award more.
She has no room left on her shelf for another trophy.
She is ashamed of how badly she played this season.
She is planning to give the trophy to Priya the next day.
explanation: Evidence: "You were the real MVP" (para 5) and "Maybe later." Maya hides the trophy because she believes Priya earned it. The shelf choice fails because the passage says there is an "empty spot" waiting for it.

The lake was a sheet of hammered tin by the time Grandpa finally cast his line. He settled into the folding chair and cleared his throat.

"Did I ever tell you about the pike I caught in '71? Big as a canoe paddle."

Theo had heard the story at Easter. He had heard it again on the drive up that morning. He reeled in slowly, watching the lure wobble toward the dock.

"No," he said. "How big?"

Grandpa's hands spread wide, and his face lit up the way it did in old photographs. He told it all: the rain, the broken net, the way the fish had looked him straight in the eye. Theo asked questions in all the right places.

When the story ended, Grandpa gazed out at the water for a long time. "Your dad never liked fishing," he said quietly. "Glad somebody does."

Theo didn't like fishing much either. He cast again anyway.

choices: He has honestly forgotten the story.
He wants Grandpa to enjoy telling it again.
He hopes to catch Grandpa telling it wrong.
He thinks the story will end differently this time.
explanation: Evidence: "Theo had heard the story at Easter" (para 3) and "Theo asked questions in all the right places." (para 5) He pretends it is new so Grandpa can have fun telling it. The forgotten choice fails because he heard it that very morning.

"Try not to trip over the ball," Dani said as I climbed out of the car. "It's round. It rolls. Just a heads-up."

"Thanks," I said. "Super helpful."

She was already looking at her phone. My sister had been sixteen for three weeks and acted like driving me anywhere was a punishment invented specifically for her.

Tryouts lasted two hours. I missed an easy pass in the first drill and felt my face go hot for the rest of the afternoon. When the coach finally blew the whistle, I walked to the parking lot slowly, expecting an empty space and a text that said "walk home."

Dani's car was in the same spot. The engine was off. Her phone was face-down on the dashboard, and there was a sports drink in the cupholder, the blue kind I like, still cold.

"Took you long enough," she said. "Get in."

choices: She is annoyed that she had to wait so long.
She feels guilty and plans to apologize for teasing him.
She cares about her brother more than her words show.
She wants to become a soccer coach.
explanation: Evidence: "Dani's car was in the same spot" (para 5) and "the blue kind I like, still cold." (para 5) She waited and brought his favorite drink, even though she talks tough. The annoyed choice is too literal; "Took you long enough" (para 6) is teasing, and her actions say the opposite.

Without the furniture, Rosa's bedroom looked bigger and somehow smaller at the same time. Her footsteps echoed. Pale rectangles on the wall showed where her posters had been, as if the room were keeping a list of everything she had taken from it.

Her father appeared in the doorway with the last box. "Ready, kiddo?"

She wasn't. She ran her thumb along the doorframe, over the pencil lines that marked her height on every birthday since she was four. The top line, from March, was almost level with her father's shoulder.

"Can we take this?" she asked.

He laughed, then saw her face and stopped. He set the box down, pulled a tape measure from his pocket, and knelt beside the doorframe. One by one, he read the numbers aloud, and Rosa wrote each one on the back of her hand in blue ink.

In the car, she kept her fist closed the whole way to the new house.

choices: the walls were dirty and needed a fresh coat of paint

Rosa had taken things that were not hers

explanation: Evidence: "Pale rectangles on the wall showed where her posters had been." (para 1) Each empty spot reminds her of something that is gone. The dirty-walls choice is too literal; the line is about how the room feels to Rosa, not about cleaning.

The new kid, Arturo, eats lunch at the end of the table by the window, and every day he sets up a little magnetic chess board next to his tray. Nobody plays with him. Honestly, I don't see why anyone would. Chess is for people who don't have friends.

I have friends. Well, I had Derek, until Derek made the travel baseball team and started sitting with them.

Today Arturo moved his knight, frowned, and moved it back. He was playing both sides. That's the saddest thing I've ever seen, I told myself, and I watched for twenty minutes to make sure.

When the bell rang, he caught me looking. "You play?" he asked.

"No," I said. Then, because my mouth apparently works without me: "My grandpa taught me. A little. A long time ago."

He turned the board around so the white pieces faced my seat. "Tomorrow, then."

I didn't say yes. But I didn't say no, either.

choices: The narrator seems lonely himself since losing Derek's company.
The narrator is secretly the best chess player in the whole school.
Arturo actually has many friends.
The narrator has never seen a game of chess.
explanation: Evidence: "I have friends. Well, I had Derek, until Derek made the travel baseball team." (para 2) He mocks people without friends while he has just lost his own. The never-seen-chess choice fails because "My grandpa taught me." (para 5)

By April the wind had stopped feeling like weather and started feeling like a houseguest who would not leave. It rattled the windows at breakfast. It hissed under the door at supper. Every morning Ma swept a little dune off the kitchen floor, and every evening it was back.

Lucy's job was the tomatoes. She had planted them in coffee cans along the porch rail, twelve cans, and she carried water to them from the pump in a bucket that sloshed against her shins. Pa said it was a waste of good water. Ma said nothing, but she saved the dishwater in a pan and set it by the porch steps.

On Sunday a dust cloud rolled in from the west, black as a bruise, and the family hid inside with wet towels over their faces. When it passed, Lucy ran out to the porch. Eleven cans were buried. One small green stem stood up out of the twelfth, bent but not broken.

She went to get the bucket.

choices: friendly company for the family
constant and unwelcome
gentle and pleasant
blowing only once in a while
explanation: Evidence: "It rattled the windows at breakfast. It hissed under the door at supper." (para 1) The wind is there all day, like a guest who stays too long. The friendly choice fails because a guest "who would not leave" (para 1) is someone you want gone.

An octopus has no bones, no shell, and very little protection from the many fish, seals, and eels that want to eat it. What it does have is one of the most remarkable disguise systems in the animal world.

Just beneath an octopus's skin lie thousands of tiny sacs of color called chromatophores. Each sac is surrounded by muscles. When the muscles squeeze or relax, the sac opens or closes, changing the color of that spot of skin in less than a second. Some octopuses can also raise small bumps on their skin, making smooth skin look rough like a rock or coral.

What puzzles scientists is that most octopuses are believed to be colorblind. Their eyes have only one type of color-sensing cell, yet they match their surroundings with astonishing accuracy. One possible explanation is that their skin itself contains light-sensing proteins similar to those found in eyes. If so, an octopus may, in a sense, "see" with its skin.

Researchers are still testing this idea. For now, the octopus remains a master of disguise that keeps its biggest secret well hidden.

In 1817, New York governor DeWitt Clinton proposed digging a canal more than 360 miles long, connecting the Hudson River at Albany to Lake Erie at Buffalo. Many people thought the idea was absurd. At the time, the longest canal in America was less than 30 miles long. Critics mocked the project as "Clinton's Ditch."

Construction took eight years. Workers, many of them Irish immigrants, dug much of the canal by hand with shovels, picks, and horse-drawn plows. Because few American engineers had canal experience, many learned on the job, solving problems as they appeared.

When the Erie Canal opened in 1825, the results silenced most critics. Before the canal, moving a ton of goods from Buffalo to New York City cost about $100 and took weeks. Afterward, it cost roughly $10 and took about eight days. Farmers in the Midwest could suddenly sell crops on the East Coast, and New York City grew into the busiest port in the nation.

The "ditch" that people once laughed at had changed the shape of American trade.

A leaf's green comes from chlorophyll, the chemical plants use to turn sunlight into food. Leaves also contain yellow and orange chemicals called carotenoids, but in summer there is so much chlorophyll that it masks them. As days shorten in the fall, trees stop producing chlorophyll. The green fades, and the yellows and oranges that were underneath all along finally show through.

Red is different. The reds and purples of maples and sumacs come from chemicals called anthocyanins, which many trees actually produce in the fall. Scientists think anthocyanins may act like sunscreen, protecting the leaf while the tree pulls valuable nutrients out of it before it drops.

More than two million gallons of molasses poured into the streets in a wave estimated at twenty-five feet high, moving at about thirty-five miles per hour. It knocked buildings off their foundations and swept up horses, wagons, and people. Twenty-one people died, and about 150 were injured.

The disaster may sound almost comic today, but it was no accident of nature. The tank had leaked from the start, so badly that neighbors collected the dripping molasses for their kitchens. Instead of fixing the problem, the company painted the tank brown so the leaks would be harder to see. The man in charge of building the tank was not an engineer and could not read blueprints.

After years of court hearings, the company was found responsible. The case helped lead to new rules requiring that plans for large structures be checked and signed by qualified engineers. A sticky, strange tragedy became a lesson in public safety.

If you have ever lain awake at 11 p.m. feeling wide awake, only to be nearly impossible to wake at 7 a.m., your body may not be lazy. It may be right on schedule.

During the teenage years, the brain begins releasing melatonin, the hormone that signals it is time to sleep, about one to two hours later than it did in childhood. As a result, many teenagers naturally feel sleepy later at night. Yet most still need eight to ten hours of sleep, and school start times rarely shift to match.

That missing sleep matters. While we sleep, the brain sorts through the day's experiences and strengthens the memories it decides to keep. Students who study and then sleep well tend to remember more than those who stay up late cramming. Sleep also helps control mood and attention, which is why a short night can make even simple tasks feel frustrating.

Some school districts have moved high school start times later. Several studies of these districts found that students slept longer, attended class more often, and were less likely to fall asleep at their desks.

In the early 1800s, the crumbling cliffs near Lyme Regis, on England's southern coast, were dangerous places. Landslides were common, especially after winter storms. They were also among the best places in the country to find fossils, and no one searched them more skillfully than Mary Anning.

Anning's family was poor. After her father died, she and her brother sold fossils to tourists to help pay the family's debts. Around the age of twelve, Mary helped uncover one of the first complete skeletons of an ichthyosaur, a sea reptile that had lived millions of years earlier. Later she found a nearly complete plesiosaur, a creature so strange that one famous scientist at first suspected it was a fake.

Despite her discoveries, Anning was not allowed to join Britain's leading scientific society, which did not admit women. Wealthy collectors often bought her fossils and described them in scientific papers without mentioning her name. Still, many experts quietly came to her for advice, because she understood the ancient creatures better than almost anyone.

Today she is recognized as one of the founders of paleontology, the study of fossils.
